title: The Sharpe Pint: SpaceX's Trillion-Dollar Catch, the Fed's New Regime, and the Great Treasury Divorce

opening_mood.text: Morning. Grab a coffee, or if you are reading this after a brutal day on the desk, a pint of something cold. We have got a packed slate today: Elon is trying to pull off the biggest heist in capital markets history, Jensen Huang wants you to stop clicking on apps, and the UK economy is doing its best impression of a frozen engine. Let us get into it.

content.text: SpaceX's $1.75T IPO: The S-1 Has a Massive Catch

SpaceX is targeting a Nasdaq listing on June 12 under the ticker SPCX, aiming to raise up to $80 billion at a valuation of $1.75 trillion to $2 trillion. It would be the largest IPO in history, easily beating Saudi Aramco's $29.4 billion. But the S-1 reveals that 78% ($62.8 billion) of the proceeds are already spoken for by insiders, vendors, and debt repayment (including Valor Equity Partners, Musk's X Corp, xAI investors, and Echostar). This leaves less than $18 billion for actual expansion. Meanwhile, SpaceX posted a massive $4.28 billion net loss in Q1 2026 alone, driven by its new AI division, which spent $12.7 billion of its $21 billion capex on building data centres for xAI.

Why it matters: This is a classic 'hype vs. fundamentals' battle. Morningstar initiated coverage with a $780 billion valuation—a massive 48% discount to the private market valuation. To drum up demand, retail investors are being allocated 30% of the float, which is three times the normal mega-cap norm.

The City angle: For asset managers and equity research analysts, this is a masterclass in financial engineering. Elon is essentially using SpaceX's highly successful and profitable Starlink business (which generated $11.4 billion of its $18.7 billion 2025 revenue) to fund his massive AI infrastructure ambitions at xAI, while diluting public market investors to pay off existing insiders.

What to say: 'Are we buying a world-class satellite internet business in Starlink, or are we just funding Elon's xAI data centre bills? When 78% of the IPO proceeds are already spoken for by insiders, you aren't investing in the future of space—you're cashing out the old guard.'
Nvidia's RTX Spark: Jensen Wants to Kill the App

At Computex 2026 in Taipei, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang unveiled the 'RTX Spark' superchip, a 1-petaflop system-on-chip (SoC) featuring a 20-core ARM CPU and a Blackwell GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. Slim laptops and desktops from Dell, Lenovo, HP, ASUS, and Microsoft Surface will launch this autumn.

Why it matters: It represents a shift from 'running apps' to 'running local personal AI agents' that do the work for you. It also signals Nvidia's aggressive push into the consumer PC market, taking on Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm's ARM chips.

The City angle: Nvidia is trying to lock in its CUDA ecosystem at the edge (local PCs) just as it did in the data centre. If developers build agentic apps for RTX Spark, Nvidia's moat becomes completely unassailable.

What to say: 'Jensen's pitch is that we're moving from clicking apps to telling our PCs what to do. If RTX Spark successfully brings agentic AI to the local device, it secures Nvidia's consumer moat and puts massive pressure on Intel and AMD, who are already lagging in the AI PC race.'
HPE Smashes Q2: The AI Hardware Gold Rush Continues

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) reported record Q2 fiscal 2026 results. Revenue hit $10.7 billion (up 40% YoY, beating estimates by 9.6%), and non-GAAP EPS was $0.79 (up 108% YoY, beating the $0.53 forecast). The stock jumped over 9% in after-hours trading.

Why it matters: AI systems bookings reached $1.8 billion in the quarter, with cumulative AI bookings hitting $16.4 billion and a $5.9 billion backlog entering Q3. The Juniper Networks integration is also running ahead of schedule.
The City angle: This is proof that the physical buildout of AI infrastructure isn't slowing down. HPE's results show that enterprise demand for AI servers and networking is highly durable.

What to say: 'HPE's 40% revenue jump and massive AI backlog show that the hardware layer of the AI trade is still printing cash. It's not just Nvidia; the system integrators and networking guys are capturing serious value.'
UK Gilts and the Great Labour Freeze

The UK is facing a tough economic backdrop. Ofgem announced a 13% rise in energy bills due to the ongoing conflict in Iran, meaning headline inflation will likely remain above the Bank of England's target for a fifth consecutive year. BoE Governor Andrew Bailey indicated rate cuts are off the table. UK 10-year gilt yields remain elevated, the highest among advanced economies.

Why it matters: The UK labour market is stagnating, with resignation rates dropping to 0.55% as workers cling to roles due to fewer vacancies, higher employer taxes, and automation fears. Meanwhile, Chancellor Rachel Reeves has ordered ministers to prioritise domestic contracts in steel and AI.
The City angle: For asset managers, the 'higher-for-longer' narrative in the UK is firmly entrenched. The gilt-bund spread is widening, and the lack of labour mobility is a drag on productivity.

What to say: 'With UK resignation rates down to 0.55% and energy bills up 13%, the consumer is squeezed and the labour market is frozen. Bailey's hands are tied by the Iran energy shock, making gilts a painful but high-yielding hold compared to bunds or treasuries.'
Oil Whipsaws as US-Iran Ceasefire Fails to Hold

Brent crude and global markets experienced high volatility after Iranian state media reported that Tehran suspended nuclear and peace negotiations with the US, blaming Israeli operations against Hezbollah in Lebanon. This threatened a fragile US-Iran ceasefire.

Why it matters: The US had recently designated Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) under its 'Economic Fury' campaign, and Iran's threat to close the Strait of Hormuz has amplified supply disruption fears.

The City angle: Macro desks are pricing in a higher geopolitical risk premium. The suspension of talks means the energy-driven inflation shock is unlikely to subside soon, complicating central bank paths.

What to say: 'The suspension of US-Iran talks shows that the geopolitical risk premium in crude isn't going anywhere. If the Strait of Hormuz toll system or threats of closure escalate, we're looking at a structural bid under oil that keeps central banks hawkish.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Morning After: Record Highs and Geopolitical Whiplash

If you went to sleep on Monday thinking the market was invincible, Tuesday morning is offering a gentle, caffeine-deprived reality check. The S&P 500 closed at a fresh record high of 7,599.52 on Monday—practically begging for a round of drinks to celebrate cracking the 7,600 mark—while the Nasdaq 100 ticked up 0.35%. But as we shake off the morning fog, US futures are drifting slightly lower, with S&P 500 futures down about 0.1%, as traders try to digest a dizzying mix of Middle Eastern headlines, hot manufacturing data, and the looming shadow of a brand-new Fed regime.
Crude Spikes, Trump Tweets, and the Ceasefire Dance

The real drama over the last 24 hours has been in the commodities pits. WTI crude oil surged a massive 5.7% on Monday to cross $92 a barrel, with Brent hitting $94, after Iran suspended indirect negotiations with the US in protest of Israel's military actions in Lebanon. For a moment, the City's inflation models were flashing red. But in true 2026 fashion, a series of posts from President Trump on Truth Social claiming that peace talks are actually continuing at a 'rapid pace' and that Israel and Hezbollah have agreed to dial back the fighting has calmed nerves. Brent has since eased back by 1.2%, trading just below $94. It is a classic reminder of how binary geopolitical risk has become: one headline and you are pricing in an energy shock; another, and it is back to the AI races.
Under the Hood: The 'Higher for Longer' Reality

Away from the geopolitical noise, the macro data continues to paint a picture of a US economy that simply refuses to roll over. The ISM Manufacturing PMI landed at a robust 54.0 on Monday, comfortably beating expectations. While that is great news for corporate earnings, it is a headache for the rates desk, keeping the 'delayed rate cuts' theme front and centre. This is particularly spicy because we are now officially in the Kevin Warsh era at the Federal Reserve. Sworn in as the 17th Fed Chair on May 22, Warsh is known to be a balance-sheet hawk who wants a 'regime change' to tackle sticky inflation. His first FOMC meeting on June 17 is fast approaching, and the market is already pricing in a more disciplined, less dovish central bank. US 10-year Treasury yields, which have been on an upward march, found a tiny bit of relief on Tuesday morning, easing 3 basis points to 4.43%, but the structural bias remains tilted toward higher borrowing costs.
The AI Ecosystem Broadens

If you think the AI trade is getting tired, Nvidia's Jensen Huang has other ideas. Speaking at Computex, Huang casually dropped that chipmaker Marvell Technology could be the 'next trillion-dollar company', sending Marvell's stock soaring over 23% in US premarket trading. This highlights a massive trend we are seeing in asset management this year: the rotation away from the pure 'hyperscalers' (the big tech firms writing the massive capex cheques) toward the 'suppliers'. Investors are realising that building data centres requires massive cooling infrastructure, server connectivity, and power distribution. Year-to-date, these infrastructure suppliers have dramatically outperformed the chip buyers. Hewlett Packard Enterprise also gave this thesis a boost, jumping in after-hours trading after beating revenue and earnings forecasts on the back of surging AI infrastructure demand.
FX, Crypto, and a 23-Hour Trading Day

In the currency markets, the US dollar remains the undisputed king, supported by high yields and economic resilience. The Dollar Index is holding firm at 99.16, while USD/JPY is flirting with the 160 mark, trading around 159.72. Over in crypto land, the higher-for-longer rates outlook is taking some of the shine off digital assets. Bitcoin has slipped below $70,000 for the first time in two months, showing that even the most speculative corners of the market aren't entirely immune to rising real yields. Finally, for those who think the trading day isn't long enough, the SEC has officially approved Cboe's proposal to launch 23x5 US equities trading on its EDGX exchange. Set to launch in December, it means global investors—especially retail traders in Asia—will soon be able to trade US stocks almost around the clock. Great for market efficiency, perhaps less great for the sleep schedules of global macro desks.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The IFRS 16 Lease Illusion

content.text: The IFRS 16 Lease Illusion (Or: Why EV/EBITDA is Lying to You)

Let's talk about lease accounting. Yes, I know—mentioning 'IFRS 16' at the pub is a quick way to ensure you drink alone. But bear with me, because this single accounting standard is responsible for some of the most common valuation blunders made by junior analysts and seasoned PMs alike. If you're looking at retail, airlines, restaurants, or any sector that rents its real estate, your EV/EBITDA multiples are probably lying to you.
The Magic Trick: How Rent Disappeared

Before 2019 (under the old IAS 17 rules), if a company leased its premises—say, a chain of pubs across London—the rent was simply treated as an operating expense. It sat in the income statement, reduced EBITDA, and the lease itself was 'off-balance sheet,' hidden away in the footnotes. Simple.

Then the accounting gods decided this was a bit of a cheat. Under IFRS 16 (and ASC 842 in the US), operating leases were brought onto the balance sheet. Now, when a company signs a lease, it must record a 'Right-of-Use' (ROU) asset and a corresponding 'Lease Liability' (the present value of all future rent payments).

But here is where the income statement gets weird. The actual rent payment is no longer an operating expense. Instead, it is split into two things: depreciation of the ROU asset, and interest expense on the lease liability. Because depreciation and interest sit below the EBITDA line, EBITDA magically jumps up, even though the company hasn't made a single extra penny in actual cash.
Let's Run the Numbers
Imagine 'The Pint & Anchor' pub chain. Under the old rules (or if we adjust to ignore IFRS 16):

items: Revenue: £100m
Operating costs (staff, beer, etc.): £50m
Rent: £10m
Traditional Net Debt (bank loans): £100m
Market Cap: £300m
Enterprise Value (EV): £400m (Market Cap + Net Debt)
EV/EBITDA Multiple: 10.0x (£400m / £40m)

content.text: Now, let's look at the exact same company under IFRS 16. The £10m rent is gone from operating costs. Instead, it's split into £8m of depreciation and £2m of interest. Meanwhile, the present value of those future rent payments is calculated as a £60m lease liability.

items: New EBITDA: £50m (the £10m rent is no longer subtracted)
New Net Debt: £160m (we must add the £60m lease liability to the £100m bank debt)
New EV: £460m (Market Cap + New Net Debt)
New EV/EBITDA Multiple: 9.2x (£460m / £50m)

content.text: Look at that. The underlying business is completely identical. The cash flow is the same. Yet the EV/EBITDA multiple has dropped from 10.0x to 9.2x. It looks cheaper, but it isn't.
Why the Multiple Compresses (The Technical Nuance)

Why did the multiple drop? It comes down to the 'implied lease multiple.' In our example, we added £60m of lease liability to the numerator (EV) and £10m of rent back to the denominator (EBITDA). That means we valued the leases at an implied multiple of 6.0x (£60m / £10m). Because 6.0x is lower than the company's original multiple of 10.0x, blending them together dragged the overall multiple down to 9.2x.

If the lease liability had been £120m (an implied lease multiple of 12.0x), the new EV would be £520m, and the new multiple would have risen to 10.4x. The direction of the change depends entirely on whether the lease multiple is higher or lower than the company's pre-lease multiple.
Why This Matters in the Real World

items: Screening Bias: If you run a quantitative screen for 'cheap' stocks using unadjusted EV/EBITDA, you will end up heavily overweight in companies with massive lease liabilities (like retailers or airlines) because their multiples look artificially compressed.

Peer Comparisons: Comparing a retailer that leases all its shops (e.g., JD Sports) to one that owns its properties (e.g., Tesco) is completely broken unless you adjust. Tesco's EBITDA is naturally higher because they don't pay rent, but they have higher capex. You aren't comparing apples to apples.

LBOs and Debt Covenants: Private equity sponsors and lenders care deeply about this. Many debt covenants are still calculated on 'Frozen GAAP' (pre-IFRS 16) or use 'EBITDAR' (EBITDA before Rent) to avoid accounting distortions.

content.text: The Classic Interview Trap

If you are interviewing for an asset management, private equity, or investment banking role, this is a prime target. An interviewer might ask: 'If a company decides to sell its headquarters and lease it back, what happens to its EV/EBITDA multiple?'

A lazy candidate will say: 'EBITDA goes down because they now pay rent, so the multiple goes up.' But a sharp candidate will say: 'Under IFRS 16, the rent is capitalised. EBITDA actually increases because the rent is treated as depreciation and interest, but EV also increases because of the lease liability. The impact on the multiple depends on the implied lease multiple relative to the company's existing EV/EBITDA multiple.' That answer instantly puts you in the top 5% of candidates.
What to Say at the Pub (or in your Morning Meeting)

If we're screening retail or consumer stocks on raw EV/EBITDA without adjusting for lease liabilities, we're not finding cheap businesses—we're just finding businesses that rent a lot of real estate. We should be looking at EV/EBITDAR or fully adjusting EV to include lease liabilities to get a true picture of leverage and valuation.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Mamba & State Space Models

content.text: Mamba & State Space Models

If you've spent any time trying to apply modern deep learning to financial time series, you've probably hit a wall. You want to capture long-range dependencies—say, how a macro announcement three hours ago affects order book dynamics right now. LSTMs are too forgetful, compressing everything into a single hidden state. Transformers are brilliant at memory, but they have a massive, expensive flaw: quadratic complexity. Try feeding a Transformer a few thousand steps of high-frequency tick data, and your GPU will start sounding like a Boeing 747 taking off from Heathrow. Enter Mamba and Selective State Space Models (SSMs).

Mamba is a modern reimagining of classical state-space models (think Kalman filters on steroids). Instead of the attention mechanism where every single time-step looks at every other time-step, Mamba uses a selective mechanism that decides what to keep and what to discard at each step. It processes sequences in linear time while maintaining the long-range context of a Transformer. For quants, this is exactly what they have been looking for: the ability to ingest massive, high-frequency datasets in real-time without needing a sovereign wealth fund's budget to pay for the compute.
The Finance Use Case: High-Frequency Volatility & Price Prediction

In high-frequency trading (HFT) and crypto markets, the order book moves at millisecond speeds. Traditional models struggle to balance the microstructural noise of the last 10 seconds with the broader regime shifts of the last 10 hours. A Mamba-based architecture can ingest long sequences of limit order book (LOB) states, order flows, and trade volumes. Because of its linear complexity, it can run inference in microseconds, making it actually viable for real-time execution algorithms and volatility forecasting.
A Quick Look at the Code
Here is a conceptual look at how you would set up a simple Mamba-based forecasting block in PyTorch, leveraging the selective state-space layers:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from mamba_ssm import Mamba

class MambaForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, d_model, d_state, d_conv, expand, output_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_projection = nn.Linear(input_dim, d_model)
        self.mamba = Mamba(
            d_model=d_model,
            d_state=d_state,
            d_conv=d_conv,
            expand=expand
        )
        self.output_projection = nn.Linear(d_model, output_dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.input_projection(x)
        x = self.mamba(x)
        out = self.output_projection(x[:, -1, :])
        return out
The Paper Trail

This isn't just theoretical. A paper published in early 2026, 'CryptoMamba-SSM: Linear Complexity State Space Models for Cryptocurrency Volatility Prediction' by Zhao et al., put this exact concept to the test. They benchmarked a Mamba-based state space model against LSTMs, GRUs, and Transformers on high-frequency Bitcoin data. The results? CryptoMamba-SSM achieved up to a 23.7% reduction in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and a 31.2% improvement in directional accuracy over traditional baselines. More importantly, it did so with a fraction of the computational footprint, proving that you don't need to sacrifice speed for accuracy when modeling complex, regime-switching volatility.
The Pub / Interview Angle

If you want to sound like the smartest person in the room (or at least the most technically sharp at the pub), drop this into a conversation about sequence modeling: 'Everyone in the City is still obsessed with LSTMs for time series or trying to force-fit Transformers. But if you're dealing with high-frequency tick data or long-horizon macro variables, Transformers are a computational bottleneck. Selective State Space Models like Mamba are the real edge right now—they give you the long-range memory of attention mechanisms but with linear complexity. It's basically Kalman filtering meets deep learning, and it actually runs in real-time.'
The Catch (Risks & Limitations)

Before you go rewriting your entire trading library in Mamba, there are a few caveats. First, Mamba is notoriously sensitive to hyperparameter tuning, particularly the discretization step size which controls how continuous-time dynamics are mapped to discrete steps. Get this wrong, and the model completely loses its grip on temporal dynamics. Second, the software ecosystem is still young. Mamba relies on highly optimized CUDA and Triton kernels to achieve its speed. If your production stack is CPU-only or relies on legacy C++ wrappers without robust GPU support, deploying Mamba is going to be an absolute nightmare for your engineering team.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Divorce of the Dollar and the Treasury

For decades, the global financial system has operated on a simple, comforting assumption: the US Dollar and US Treasuries are a package deal. If the world goes to pot, investors buy both. Because of this 'exorbitant privilege', the US government has enjoyed a 'convenience yield'—essentially a discount on its borrowing costs because investors value the safety and liquidity of Treasuries so much they are willing to accept lower yields. But a landmark paper from Wenxin Du (Harvard Business School), Ritt Keerati (Federal Reserve Board), and Jesse Schreger (Columbia Business School) reveals that this happy marriage is officially over.
The Paper

'Decoupling Dollar and Treasury Privilege' (NBER Working Paper 35000 / Federal Reserve IFDP 1427) is a masterclass in empirical macro-finance. It uses Covered Interest Parity (CIP) deviations to measure the 'specialness' of both the greenback and US government debt, and the results are eye-opening.
Why It Matters: The Great Decoupling

The authors show that since the Global Financial Crisis, and accelerating rapidly in the 2020s, the convenience yields of the dollar and Treasuries have completely decoupled. The dollar is still king: its global convenience yield remains positive, averaging about 20 basis points across G10 currencies from 2021 to 2025. Foreign banks and corporates still desperately need dollar funding to grease the wheels of global trade, and they are willing to pay a premium for it.

But Treasuries? They have lost their crown. The convenience yield on 5-year Treasuries actually turned negative in 2012 and has plummeted since, averaging -26 basis points since 2021 (compared to -7 bps in 2012–20). Short-term Treasuries (3-month and 1-year) joined the sub-zero club in 2023. In plain English: on a currency-hedged basis, the US Treasury now has to pay a higher yield to attract investors than other G10 sovereigns like Germany. Treasuries have gone from being a 'safe haven' to being 'inconvenient'.
The Culprit: A Flood of Paper

Why has this happened? It is a simple story of supply and demand, mixed with regulatory plumbing. The sheer volume of US debt issuance has flooded the market. The authors estimate that a 1% increase in the US debt-to-GDP ratio is associated with a 0.37 to 0.86 basis point drop in Treasury convenience. Because traditional long-only investors cannot absorb this mountain of paper, the slack is taken up by leveraged financial intermediaries (like hedge funds doing the infamous Treasury basis trade). But these intermediaries face strict balance-sheet and Value-at-Risk (VaR) constraints. To hold this debt, they demand a premium, which collapses swap spreads and drives Treasury convenience yields deep into negative territory.

"Despite the dollar being special, there is something not so desirable about Treasury securities that now the Department of Treasury actually has to issue at a higher yield on the currency risk hedged basis compared to its G-10 currency pairs... If you flood the market with this instrument, it has lost its specialness, and the price does reflect that." — Professor Wenxin Du
The Sharpe Take

This paper is essential reading because it provides the academic proof for what macro traders have been feeling in their bones: the plumbing of the Treasury market is clogged. It explains why swap spreads have been deeply negative for years, and why the leveraged basis trade has become a structural necessity rather than a temporary arbitrage. If the US fiscal trajectory does not stabilise, the US government will face structurally higher borrowing costs—not because of the Fed, but because the world is demanding a premium to hold its paper.
How to Use This at Work

items: In interviews: If you are interviewing for a macro hedge fund, asset manager, or fixed-income desk, drop this paper. It shows you understand that 'risk-free' is a relative term and that sovereign debt pricing is heavily constrained by intermediary balance sheets.

Over a pint: When a colleague starts rambling about the 'demise of the dollar' or BRICS currency threats, set them straight. The dollar is doing fine; it's the Treasury market that's in trouble. The currency is still the global reserve, but the debt backing it is losing its premium.

What to skim: Skip the heavy econometric proofs and the formal mathematical modelling of the constrained global financial intermediary in Sections 5 and 6. Focus on the introduction, the empirical measurement of CIP deviations, and the charts showing the divergence.

content.text: The Curse of Knowledge: Why Your Brilliant Ideas Sound Like Erratic Table-Tapping

You have almost certainly sat through a meeting where an incredibly bright quant or tech lead spent forty minutes explaining a new model, and by slide three, the entire room had glazed over. Or perhaps you have been on the other side—pitching a brilliant investment thesis to a senior portfolio manager, only to be met with blank stares and a polite, 'Thanks, we will take a look.' It is easy to assume the audience just didn't get it. But the real culprit is a classic cognitive bias: the Curse of Knowledge.

First coined in 1989 by economists Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein, and Martin Weber in the Journal of Political Economy, the bias is simple: once you know something, you find it virtually impossible to imagine what it is like not to know it. The concept was famously demonstrated in a 1990 Stanford study by Elizabeth Newton. Participants were split into 'tappers' and 'listeners'. Tappers were asked to tap out the rhythm of well-known songs (like 'Happy Birthday') on a table, while listeners guessed the tune. The tappers predicted that listeners would guess the song correctly 50% of the time. The actual success rate? A measly 2.5%.

Why the massive disconnect? The tappers had the song humming beautifully in their own heads. To them, the taps were an obvious, melodic masterpiece. But to the listeners, who did not have the internal soundtrack, it just sounded like some bloke erratically banging his knuckles on a desk. In the City, we do this constantly. We have a beautiful, complex intellectual 'soundtrack' playing in our heads—whether it is the mechanics of a cross-currency basis swap or a machine learning alpha model—and we assume everyone else can hear it when we tap.

items: The Quant vs. PM: A quant presents a new model, talking endlessly about hyperparameter tuning and gradient boosting. The PM just hears erratic finger-tapping and thinks: 'Why should I risk my capital on this?'

The Pitch Deck: An analyst dumps a chart of 5-year swap spreads onto a slide and labels it 'Macro Outlook'. They know exactly what the chart implies because they spent three days building it. The client or MD looks at it and thinks, 'Right, and?'

The Client Update: A portfolio manager explains a quarter of underperformance by diving straight into the weeds of factor rotation, forgetting that the client is still trying to remember what a 'factor' actually is.

content.text: To break the curse, you have to actively provide the soundtrack. The easiest way to do this in your day-to-day work is to write 'headlines' instead of 'labels' on your slides and memos. Instead of labeling a slide 'Q2 Performance', write: 'Q2 Performance Fell 4% Due to FX Headwinds'. Tell them exactly what the tune is before you start tapping. Another trick is the 'Explain it to Compliance' test: if you cannot explain your trade idea or model to a colleague in HR or compliance without them looking like they want to jump out of a window, you have not simplified it enough.
One line to remember: Just because you can hear the tune in your head does not mean they can hear it through your desk-tapping.
